https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-c.text: The rain stopped in spring and never came back. From France to Czechia, this summer's harvest is withering — and depleting aid funds built for one-off disasters, not a crisis that returns every year. Climate change has made dry seasons so frequent in Europe that the aid has become routine, too: national rescue packages, topped up by EU money. Nearly all of it covers what farmers have already lost; very little goes toward surviving the next one. For all the money the EU spends on farming, none of it is guaranteed to farmers when drought hits. Every rescue is improvised, decided one at a time. And the European Commission says it can’t afford a standing fund unless capitals pay in more, which none have offered to do. Advertisement Advertisement In Czechia, just 32 millimeters of rain fell across March and April — the driest spring in more than 60 years. The heat that followed pushed field temperatures past 50 degrees Celsius. “In some cases maize fields are failing to produce anything which can be used as fodder for animals,” said Jan Doležal of the Agrarian Chamber of the Czech Republic farm lobby. He hoped the EU would pay out for the damage in the fall. How to respond to that cycle — damage first, compensation later, repeat next season — is one of the disputes running through the negotiations on the EU’s next long-term farm budget . One flashpoint is a small emergency fund inside that post-2028 budget, reserved for when markets crash — collapsing prices, gluts of cheap imports, disease outbreaks. It can pay for weather damage, but only when the Commission decides to allow it, case by case. Most governments in the drought belt want ruined harvests written in as a standard trigger. The Commission's answer: No realistic amount of euros would cover the damage. "Even 900 million” would amount to just “peanuts,” Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen told reporters in July. While that figure represents the Commission’s proposal to double the current crisis cache, he noted, “if we have to take everything on board what [countries] are asking, it would be ridiculously low.” Dry belt The EU's own drought maps show the worst of it cutting straight through the middle of the Continent. Advertisement Advertisement In Hungary, where this summer's harvests are coming in 10 to 20 percent below the five-year average, the agriculture ministry said the tools simply haven't kept up with the changing climate. Emergency aid and insurance need rebuilding for a hotter Europe, the ministry said in a statement, with more EU money behind them, so farmers get help "faster and more predictably." Commissioner Christophe Hansen wants the money to go toward longer-term solutions, rather than purely padding out farmers’ losses. | John Thys/AFP vis Getty Images Together with six other countries in the dry belt, Hungary backed a declaration in June demanding a list of changes to the emergency fund's successor. Those countries — Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Croatia and Romania — want it to cover weather damage; pay out when a farmer loses a fifth of a crop rather than a third; and provide the money before the paperwork clears. As things stand, they wrote, "relief comes too late." Commissioner Hansen wants the money to go toward longer-term solutions, rather than purely padding out farmers’ losses. Ideas include irrigation and water infrastructure to blunt the damage and an insurance push with the European Investment Bank so that bad years are covered by premiums rather than emergency funds. But “we will never find enough money,” he said, unless richer EU countries put more into the bloc’s joint budget. So far, those countries are pushing for the pot to be reduced instead. Spending strategy split Not all countries suffering drought are in favor of easier access to emergency cash. Advertisement Advertisement In France, the heat struck just as the corn flowered, and no grain formed. By mid-July, growers were mowing the plants down for animal feed. The industry expects its smallest corn crop in at least a quarter-century — down 30 percent in a single year. However, the country’s agriculture ministry said the EU’s crisis money should stay what it is: a tool for market shocks. Climate risk, the ministry said in a statement, belongs with dedicated instruments like subsidized crop insurance. For Polish Agriculture Minister Stefan Krajewski, emergency cash and tools designed to manage longer-term risk are complementary. "One shouldn't be completely replaced by the other," he said. Among farm groups, the pushback is less about prevention itself than about how it’s implemented: Farmers ordered into new practices, versus being paid to adopt them. In Germany, the Rhine has dropped so low that cargo ships sail half-loaded, driving up the cost of moving grain and feed. The German Farmers Association backs the shift toward prevention and adaptation — as long as it comes with “investment,” said chief Stefanie Sabet, “not obligation.” Clea Caulcutt contributed to this report from Paris.

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: People gathered on Garvaghy Road, a Catholic area in the largely Protestant town of Portadown, on Sunday to protest against the Orange Order march. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters View image in fullscreen People gathered on Garvaghy Road, a Catholic area in the largely Protestant town of Portadown, on Sunday to protest against the Orange Order march. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters Northern Ireland Mediation over Drumcree parade is ‘dead in the water’, say nationalists Northern Ireland secretary holding talks with both sides as Garvaghy Road group launches fresh legal challenge UK politics live – latest updates Lisa O’Carroll Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Talks to break the deadlock over the controversial Drumcree parade will continue with the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, on Wednesday as nationalist protesters declare the prospect of mediation with unionists “dead in the water”. The nationalist Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition has at the same time launched a fresh legal challenge to reimpose the almost 30-year ban on the Orange Order marching down their road, mounting fresh arguments that the Parades Commission has “materially misdirected itself”. Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the group, said his goal was “no parade, just no parade, that is what our community wants, that’s what nearly 4,000 people living in our community wants … that’s our mandate”. After his meeting with Bryant on Tuesday he told residents at the local pastoral centre that mediation was “dead in the water”. Members of the Portadown Orange Order left Drumcree church, the start point for the parade, overnight on Tuesday for the first time since the dispute over their march erupted on Sunday morning. View image in fullscreen Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said his community wanted ‘no parade’. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA They made a further attempt to walk the route down the nationalist Garvaghy Road just after 10pm on Tuesday night, accompanied by the DUP MP Carla Lockhart, and returned to the church on Wednesday morning having vowed to remain there until the police allowed them to complete the march. The Orange Order Portadown district master, Nigel Dawson, said he had “constructive” talks after his meeting with the Northern Ireland secretary over the possibility of a mediator on Tuesday night. “We look forward to the law being applied to the parade,” he added. The two groups will have further talks with Bryant on Wednesday and the Garvaghy Road court hearing is scheduled for Friday, but there is little sign of a breakthrough. The high court at a special sitting on Saturday heard that the documentation around the decision to allow the parade showed past risk assessments of disorder in relation to parade requests but none looking to the future. Under a heading on a form listing any risk of public disorder or damage to property, the commission’s information was “directed to the past”, their barrister, Denise Kiley KC, told the judge. “Nowhere do we see any assessment of future risk,” she said adding that it was “not clear who had provided this template” to the Parades Commission. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Absence of violence in Drumcree does not make standoff any less significant Read more Efforts to end the dispute, which has heightened sectarian divisions in Northern Ireland, were also brought to Dublin where Sinn Féin’s leader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, met Micheál Martin and Simon Harris, the leader and deputy leader of the Irish government. Martin has described the Parades Commission decision to allow the parade march down Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years as “incomprehensible and wrong”. McDonald said people were “gobsmacked” by the decision as it had “the potential to drag that community and society back to a very bad and very bleak days”. O’Neill has faced criticism from unionists after she and senior colleagues were among a large crowd that blockaded the road in the predominantly nationalist Garvaghy Road area on Sunday to prevent the parade from passing the route. Under parading laws in Northern Ireland , protests must be notified to, and approved by, the Parades Commission adjudication body and the gathering at the head of Garvaghy Road, that continues on Wednesday, has not yet been notified. However, police have not tried to break up the protest, fearing it could trigger violence. Bertie Ahern, the former taoiseach and co-architect of the 1998 peace deal that led to republicans and loyalists laying down their arms after 30 years of violence, warned of the dangers of returning to the “tribal past”. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/russ.text: Russia has asked Vietnam to lease its passenger jets complete with crews and maintenance, as the fleet it seized from Western lessors in 2022 deteriorates and nearly a fifth of the country's largest airlines' planes sit grounded.Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin said Moscow had proposed that Vietnamese carriers transfer aircraft to Russian airlines under wet lease — an arrangement that covers jets, crew, maintenance and insurance — and that Hanoi was studying the proposal.Vietnam's main carrier exclusively operates Airbus and Boeing aircraft, meaning any transfer to Russia would involve Western-built planes. That creates the same secondary sanctions risk that led Ethiopia to decline a similar proposal, as companies could face US penalties for facilitating the operation of sanctioned aircraft types on behalf of a Russian carrier.Approaches to other countries in Asia, Africa and the Middle East have so far produced nothing.Russia's request to Vietnam shows how far Russia's seized and cannibalised fleet of passenger jets — built on legally contested re-registrations and parts that do not meet international airworthiness standards — has deteriorated.Cobbling things togetherWhen sanctions were imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Moscow passed a law allowing airlines to re-register more than 400 foreign-leased Western aircraft domestically rather than return them to their owners.Under international aviation law, dual registration of a single aircraft is prohibited, meaning Russia's re-registrations are illegal, but the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) has no enforcement mechanism to compel their return.Lessors have filed insurance claims totalling around $8 billion (€7.1bn) to recover their losses, with many cases still ongoing.Before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, roughly 850 of Russia's 900 commercial aircraft were US and European-made Boeing or Airbus planes, of which around 85% were leased from foreign companies.With Western spare parts and technical services now sanctioned, airlines have been cannibalising the seized fleet for components, making legal matters worse.Under international airworthiness standards, every component must have a certified and traceable maintenance history.Parts stripped from aircraft cut off from Western-certified maintenance chains cannot legally be used on internationally operated aircraft.Russia's aviation regulator Rosaviatsia has been issuing its own certificates for such parts, which are not recognised by the EU or US aviation authorities.Of 673 aircraft operated by Russia's 11 largest airlines, 130 or nearly one-fifth are not in service, according to Russian industry data. The normal downtime rate is around 10%.Airlines outside the Aeroflot group are in worse shape: 93 of their 322 planes, close to a third, are idle.No kerosene for passenger jets?Fuel supply is a separate problem. Restrictions on refuelling have been introduced at at least 26 major airports, according to the outlet Verstka.At airports in St Petersburg, Kaliningrad, Yekaterinburg, Kazan, Ufa, Irkutsk and Vladivostok, fuel is rationed to the volume needed for a single flight.Restrictions are most severe in southern Russia: Sochi, Volgograd and Astrakhan have applied limits to all carriers. Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have reduced fuel production, and the government has restricted aviation fuel exports in response.The transport ministry, industry ministry and state defence conglomerate Rostec are also discussing a new passenger levy to fund the purchase and operation of domestically produced aircraft, according to Russian media.The charge is estimated at up to 500 roubles (€5.22) per domestic ticket and up to 1,000 roubles (€10.44) for international flights.Russia's domestically produced MC-21 and Tu-214 jets are significantly more expensive to operate than the Boeing and Airbus aircraft they are meant to replace, requiring state or passenger subsidies to remain viable for airlines.Analysts warn that higher fares could reduce passenger numbers and cut airline revenues.

https://telex.hu/after/2026/10/16/janesc.text: Menü Kereső A Megasztárban T. Dannyt plágiummal vádoló rapper a Magyar Honvédség tartalékos őrvezetője After Fotó: TV2 Bányász Dorka Az idei Megasztár egyik botrányhőse, Litvai János, művésznevén Janesco nem először vett részt a tehetségkutatóban, korábban Bartos Cs. István oldalán tűnt fel a Cretins nevű formáció tagjaként. Litvai ezúttal egyedül érkezett a tehetségkutató válogatójára, plágiummal vádolta meg T. Danny zsűritagot. A Megasztár új évadában Litvai azt állította, hogy az underground zenében ő korszakalkotó ember, majd Mozarthoz hasonlította magát. Elmondta, hogy azért jött a műsorba, mert van egy rendezetlen ügye az egyik zsűritaggal. Múltkor itt voltam Bartossal, hogy szembesítsem a Danit. T. Danny ellopta az egyik beatemet! Kimenekült a színpadról, mint egy gyáva nyuszi – mondta a versenyző, akit a zsűritag azonnal felismert, és azt mondta, „istenem, visszaengedték ezt a hülyegyereket”. Az adás után egy olvasónk jelezte, hogy tudomása szerint Litvai a Magyar Honvédség kötelékébe tartozik. Kérdéseket küldtünk a Honvédelmi Minisztériumnak, válaszul megerősítették, hogy Litvai János valóban tartalékos őrvezetőként teljesít szolgálatot, szerepléséről azonban a vonatkozó szabályokat figyelmen kívül hagyva előzetesen nem tájékoztatta elöljáróit. Közölték továbbá, hogy az illetékes területvédelmi ezred vizsgálatot indított az ügyben, és ennek alapján dönt a tartalékos katona további jogviszonyáról. Megkerestük a műsorban fellépő Litvait is, aki elismerte, hogy állományban van, azonban azt állította, hogy a Megasztár műsorának forgatásakor még nem tartozott a Honvédség kötelékébe, így nem volt szüksége engedélyre a szerepléshez. A zenei tevékenysége szerinte a magánéletéhez és civil tevékenységéhez tartozik, katonai kötelezettségeit viszont elsődlegesnek tekinti, a szolgálati szabályokat pedig betartja. Litvai nem sokkal később a Telexnek adott válaszait megpróbálta visszavonni, de a sajtószabadságról és a médiatartalmak alapvető szabályairól szóló 2010. évi CIV. törvény 15. §-a értelmében tilos visszaélni a nyilvános közlésre szánt nyilatkozatok vagy szereplések beleegyezésével. Ezt követően újabb kérdéseket küldtünk a Honvédelmi Minisztériumnak arról, hogy reagáljanak arra az állításra, hogy Litvai még a honvédséghez való csatlakozása előtt szerepelt a műsorban, illetve hogy összeegyeztethetőnek találják-e Litvai szereplését és zenei munkásságát a katonaságnál végzett munkájával. A Honvédelmi Minisztériumtól azt a választ kaptuk, hogy folyamatban van a vizsgálat, ezért annak lezárásáig további részletekről és a vizsgálat esetleges következményeiről nem áll módjukban tájékoztatást adni. Az biztos, hogy Litvai internetes megjelenése, zenei karrierje és tehetségkutatós szereplése visszamenőleg nem egyezik meg a Magyar Honvédség szigorú etikai kódexével , amely alapján a katonáknak a magánéletükben is komoly szabályokat kell követniük. A szabályok szerint: Nem lehet olyan munkát, feladatot elvállalni, amely megvalósítása olyan magatartást és megnyilvánulásokat feltételez, amelyek ellentétesek az etikai kódexben ajánlott elvárásokkal. Minden élethelyzetben tudatában van annak, hogy személyén keresztül ítélik meg az általa képviselt szervezetet és a Magyar Honvédséget. Kerülnie kell azokat az élethelyzeteket, amelyek alkalmasak személye, szolgálati helye, valamint a katonai szolgálat negatív megítélésére, vagy amelyek alapjául szolgálhatnak szóbeszédnek, rosszindulatú híresztelésnek. Litvai a katonai szolgálata mellett és a Megasztáros szereplése óta egyébként egy új dalt is kihozott T.Bani címmel, amiben a zsűritagot továbbra is plágiummal vádolja. Amennyiben választ kapunk a Magyar Honvédségtől arra, milyen eredménnyel zárult le a vizsgálat, beszámolunk róla. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Friss az Afteren

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: Aproximativ 360 de camioane așteaptă în coloană la Punctul de Trecere a Frontierei Siret pentru a ieși din România către Ucraina. Aglomerația este provocată de creșterea numărului de transporturi înaintea sărbătorilor de iarnă și de capacitatea limitată a părții ucrainene de a prelua automarfare, anunță Poliția de Frontieră. Timpul de așteptare este mai mare decât de obicei deoarece autoritățile ucrainene pot procesa mai puține camioane decât partea română. „În timp ce PTF Siret poate procesa, în condiții normale, aproximativ 250 de camioane în 12 ore, autoritățile ucrainene preiau, în medie, între 170 și 200 de automarfare în același interval, ceea ce determină acumularea acestora pe teritoriul României”, transmite Poliția de Frontieră. Autoritățile române discută cu cele ucrainene pentru a găsi soluții care să permită procesarea unui număr mai mare de camioane și reducerea timpilor de așteptare. „La nivelul PTF Siret sunt utilizate toate cele trei artere destinate traficului de automarfare, iar polițiștii de frontieră efectuează verificări inclusiv asupra camioanelor aflate în coloană, cu ajutorul echipamentelor mobile eDAC. În paralel, în cooperare cu Poliția Rutieră, sunt luate măsuri pentru gestionarea circulației și menținerea accesului în zona punctului de trecere”, mai precizează autoritățile. Totodată, personalul și mijloacele disponibile sunt menținute în teren pentru a adapta măsurile în funcție de evoluția traficului. Șoferii sunt sfătuiți să respecte indicațiile polițiștilor și semnalizarea rutieră temporară, să nu depășească coloana prin circulația pe contrasens și să lase liber accesul autovehiculelor de intervenție.
